props.title: How War Made English
props.subtitle: Twelve centuries. Ten wars. One language.

say: Every time you speak English, you are speaking the language of war. Invaders, raiders, conquerors and soldiers all left their words behind. And one October morning, a single battle almost wiped English off the map of its own country.
Today, about one point five billion people speak English. But it started on one small island, and it was shaped, again and again, by the people who came to fight for it.

items.label: blitz
items.note: born in the Second World War

say: The evidence is hiding in plain sight. The word sky. The word beef. The word loot. The word blitz. Each one is a scar from a different war. In this film, we follow those scars, one by one.
Chapter one. Before English. Two thousand years ago, nobody in Britain spoke a word of English. The people here were Celtic tribes, and their language was closer to modern Welsh.
Julius Caesar had come and gone. But in the year forty three, Rome returned under the emperor Claudius, and this time, the legions came to stay.
From Rome, through Gaul, and across the sea. The Romans built a new town on the river Thames, and called it Londinium. You know it today as London.
In the north, the tribes never surrendered. So in one hundred and twenty two, the emperor Hadrian ordered a wall, right across the island, to mark where Rome ended.

props.title: Words from the camps
props.subject: Where our words came from
props.body: Street: from Latin strata, a paved road. Wall: from Latin vallum, a rampart. Wine: from Latin vinum. Cheese: from Latin caseus.

say: Rome gave the future English language some of its oldest borrowed words. Street, from strata, a paved road. Wall, from vallum. Wine, from vinum. And cheese, from caseus.
Look at a map of England, and you can still see the Roman army. Manchester. Lancaster. Winchester. That ending, chester or caster, comes from the Latin word castra. It means a military camp.
Then, around the year four hundred and ten, with the empire under attack at home, the last legions sailed away. Britain was left to defend itself. And that is where English truly begins.
Chapter two. The invaders who named England.
With Rome gone, new people crossed the North Sea. Jutes from Denmark. Saxons and Angles from what is now northern Germany. The old story says they first came as hired soldiers, and then they stayed.
For more than a century, they fought the Britons for the land. Slowly, the newcomers pushed west, and the old Celtic languages retreated to Wales, Cornwall and the far north.

then.subject: landscape
then.label: Englaland, the land of the Angles

props.title: A Country Named by Its Invaders

say: The Angles gave the whole country its name. Englaland, the land of the Angles. Their language, Englisc, is the ancestor of every English word you know.
The kingdoms they built are still on the map. Essex, the East Saxons. Sussex, the South Saxons. And Wessex, the West Saxons, the kingdom that would one day save English itself.

props.title: Days of the Gods
props.subject: The names we still use
props.body: Tuesday: the day of Tiw. Wednesday: the day of Woden. Thursday: the day of Thunor, the thunder god. Friday: the day of Frige.

say: They even named your week. Tuesday is the day of Tiw. Wednesday, the day of Woden. Thursday, the day of Thunor, the god of thunder. And Friday, the day of the goddess Frige.

props.title: Plain old English
props.subject: Where our words came from
props.body: House: Old English hus. Bread: Old English bread. Water: Old English waeter. Mother: Old English modor.

say: And the simplest words of daily life are theirs too. House. Bread. Water. Mother. When you speak plainly in English, you are speaking Anglo-Saxon.

But the Anglo-Saxons were about to learn what it feels like to be invaded. Because in the summer of seven hundred and ninety three, new ships appeared off the coast of Northumbria. And the men inside them were not coming to trade.
